```
      "text": "[2406.02969] Filtered not Mixed: Stochastic Filtering-Based Online Gating for Mixture of Large Language Models\n\n# Computer Science > Machine Learning\n\narXiv:2406.02969 (cs)\n\n[Submitted on 5 Jun 2024 (v1), last revised 20 Feb 2025 (this version, v2)]\n\n# Title:Filtered not Mixed: Stochastic Filtering-Based Online Gating for Mixture of Large Language Models\n\nView PDF HTML (experimental)\n\n> Abstract:We propose MoE-F - a formalized mechanism for combining $N$ pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) for online time-series prediction by adaptively forecasting the best weighting of LLM predictions at every time step. Our mechanism leverages the conditional information in each expert's running performance to forecast the best combination of LLMs for predicting the time series in its next step. Diverging from static (learned) Mixture of Experts (MoE) methods, our approach employs time-adaptive stochastic filtering techniques to combine experts. By framing the expert selection problem as a finite state-space, continuous-time Hidden Markov model (HMM), we can leverage the Wohman-Shiryaev filter. Our approach first constructs N parallel filters corresponding to each of the $N$ individual LLMs. Each filter proposes its best combination of LLMs, given the information that they have access to. Subsequently, the N filter outputs are optimally aggregated to maximize their robust predictive power, and this update is computed efficiently via a closed-form expression, generating our ensemble predictor. Our contributions are: **(I)** the MoE-F plug-and-play filtering harness algorithm, **(II)** theoretical optimality guarantees of the proposed filtering-based gating algorithm (via optimality guarantees for its parallel Bayesian filtering and its robust aggregation steps), and **(III)** empirical evaluation and ablative results using state-of-the-art foundational and MoE LLMs on a real-world __Financial Market Movement__ task where MoE-F attains a remarkable 17\\% absolute and 48.5\\% relative F1 measure improvement over the next best performing individual LLM expert predicting short-horizon market movement based on streaming news. While transformers and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures are increasingly favored for time-series forecasting, a key gap persists: MoE models typically require complicated training with both the main forecasting loss and auxiliary load-balancing losses, along with careful routing/temperature tuning, which hinders practical adoption. In this paper, we propose a model architecture that simplifies the training process for univariate time series forecasting and effectively addresses both long- and short-term horizons, including intermittent patterns. Our approach combines sparse MoE computation with a novel attention-inspired gating mechanism that replaces the traditional one-layer softmax router. Through extensive empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that our gating design naturally promotes balanced expert utilization and achieves superior predictive accuracy without requiring the auxiliary load-balancing losses typically used in classical MoE implementations. The model achieves better performance while utilizing only a fraction of the parameters required by state-of-the-art transformer models, such as PatchTST. Furthermore, experiments across diverse datasets confirm that our MoE architecture with the proposed gating mechanism is more computationally efficient than LSTM for both long- and short-term forecasting, enabling cost-effective inference. These approaches struggle to\nefficiently capture the heterogeneous nature of time series data, where different\nsubsequences may require distinct modelings. To address these challenges, we\npropose MFMformer: Multi-resolution Mixture-of-Experts gating for Time Series\nForecasting that combines multi-scale temporal processing with MoE layers.\nMFMformer introduces two key innovations: (i) an overlapping multi-resolution\ndecomposition mechanism that splits input sequences into 50% overlapping\nchunks across multiple temporal scales, with instance normalization applied\nindependently to each scale, inspired by short-term Fourier transformation; (ii)\nMixture-of-Experts gating that uses the top-3 dominant frequencies from FFT\nanalysis to route inputs between 2 specialized expert networks, enhancing both\nrepresentational capacity and computational efficiency. Extensive benchmarks on\nlong-term and short-term time series datasets show that MFMformer shows state\u0002of-the-art results that are comparable to existing methods.\n1 INTRODUCTION\nTime series forecasting is fundamental to numerous applications across finance, meteorology,\nhealthcare, and industrial systems, where accurate predictions enable informed decision-making\nand resource optimization. However, traditional forecasting methods often struggle with real-world\ntime series that exhibit evolving statistical properties over time.\nRecent advances in Transformer-based architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017) have gained prominence\ndue to their ability to model long-range dependencies through self-attention mechanisms. Notable\ncontributions include Informer (Zhou et al., 2021), which introduces sparse attention for efficient\nlong-sequence modeling, and Autoformer (Wu et al., 2021), which employs decomposition-based\nattention with auto-correlation mechanisms to capture seasonality and trend components effectively.\nHowever, a critical challenge remains: the non-stationary nature of real-world time series data,\nwhere fundamental statistical properties such as mean, variance, and autocorrelation evolve over\ntime. We also hypothesize that the gating mechanism provides additional interpretability by identifying which expert is most relevant for each series. However, integrating heterogeneous data types into a unified forecasting framework remains an underexplored challenge. Existing multi-modal time series forecasting approaches often employ static and simplistic fusion mechanisms or yield non-interpretable representations with a limited modularity. We propose GMM-TS, a learnable gating architecture, inspired by mixture-of-experts, which dynamically integrates predictions from multiple uni-modal experts, each specialized in a distinct modality (e.g., text or numerical signals). Our method computes per-time-step expert weights using a Transformer Encoder. This enables fine-grained, interpretable fusion of multiple experts (two or more) and supports both joint and offline training modes. Extensive evaluations show that GMM-TS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across nine domains, multiple forecast horizons, and various expert configurations. We also include, for the first time, to the best of our knowledge, the option to integrate more than two experts. Our framework is efficient, extensible, and inherently interpretable.       "text": "# Repository: weifantt/Dish-TS\n\nTime Series Forecasting, Distribution Shift\n\n- Stars: 101\n- Forks: 10\n- Watchers: 101\n- Open issues: 7\n- Primary language: Python\n- Languages: Python\n- Default branch: master\n- Created: 2022-11-29T09:44:25Z\n- Last push: 2023-07-11T16:13:59Z\n- Contributors: 2 (top: weifantt, Frankfanwei)\n\n---\n\n# Dish-TS\n\nSource code for the paper,\n[\"Dish-TS: A General Paradigm for Alleviating Distribution Shift in Time Series Forecasting\"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.14829),\nin AAAI 2023.\n\n## Overview\n\nDish-TS is a general paradigm for time series forecasting against distribution shift.\n\n## Usage\n\nSimilar to [reversible instance normalization](https://openreview.net/forum?id=cGDAkQo1C0p), Dish-TS is model-agnostic such that it can be coupled with any forecasting architectures.\n\nNote that in experiments, we directly take the original data for training/evaluation to directly reflect the distribution shift in time series, and do not use preprocessing techniques (e.g., z-score normalization, min-max normalization) to process time series dataset.\n\n## Citation\n\nIf you find our work interesting, you can the paper as\n\n```text\n@inproceedings{fan2023dish,\n  title={Dish-TS: A General Paradigm for Alleviating Distribution Shift in Time Series Forecasting},\n  author={Fan, Wei and Wang, Pengyang and Wang, Dongkun and Wang, Dongjie and Zhou, Yuanchun and Fu, Yanjie},\n  booktitle={Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence},\n  volume={37},\n  number={6},\n  pages={7522--7529},\n  year={2023}\n}\n```"
```

```
      "title": "[2302.14829] Dish-TS: A General Paradigm for Alleviating Distribution Shift in Time Series Forecasting",

      "text": "[2302.14829] Dish-TS: A General Paradigm for Alleviating Distribution Shift in Time Series Forecasting\n\n -->\n\n# Computer Science > Machine Learning\n\narXiv:2302.14829 (cs)\n\n[Submitted on 22 Feb 2023 (v1), last revised 14 Mar 2023 (this version, v3)]\n\n# Title:Dish-TS: A General Paradigm for Alleviating Distribution Shift in Time Series Forecasting\n\nAuthors: Wei Fan, Pengyang Wang, Dongkun Wang, Dongjie Wang, Yuanchun Zhou, Yanjie Fu\n\nView PDF\n\n> Abstract:The distribution shift in Time Series Forecasting (TSF), indicating series distribution changes over time, largely hinders the performance of TSF models. Existing works towards distribution shift in time series are mostly limited in the quantification of distribution and, more importantly, overlook the potential shift between lookback and horizon windows. To address above challenges, we systematically summarize the distribution shift in TSF into two categories. Regarding lookback windows as input-space and horizon windows as output-space, there exist (i) intra-space shift, that the distribution within the input-space keeps shifted over time, and (ii) inter-space shift, that the distribution is shifted between input-space and output-space. Then we introduce, Dish-TS, a general neural paradigm for alleviating distribution shift in TSF. Specifically, for better distribution estimation, we propose the coefficient net (CONET), which can be any neural architectures, to map input sequences into learnable distribution coefficients. To relieve intra-space and inter-space shift, we organize Dish-TS as a Dual-CONET framework to separately learn the distribution of input- and output-space, which naturally captures the distribution difference of two spaces. In addition, we introduce a more effective training strategy for intractable CONET learning. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on several datasets coupled with different state-of-the-art forecasting models. Experimental results show Dish-TS consistently boosts them with a more than 20% average improvement.       "text": "Dish-TS: A General Paradigm for Alleviating Distribution Shift in Time Series Forecasting | Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence\n\n \n\n# Dish-TS: A General Paradigm for Alleviating Distribution Shift in Time Series Forecasting\n\n## Authors\n\n- Wei Fan University of Central Florida\n- Pengyang Wang State Key Laboratory of Internet of Things for Smart City, University of Macau\n- Dongkun Wang State Key Laboratory of Internet of Things for Smart City, University of Macau\n- Dongjie Wang University of Central Florida\n- Yuanchun Zhou Computer Network Information Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences\n- Yanjie Fu University of Central Florida\n\n## DOI:\n\nhttps://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v37i6.25914\n\n## Keywords:\n\nML: Time-Series/Data Streams, DMKM: Mining of Spatial, Temporal or Spatio-Temporal Data\n\n## Abstract\n\nThe distribution shift in Time Series Forecasting (TSF), indicating series distribution changes over time, largely hinders the performance of TSF models. Existing works towards distribution shift in time series are mostly limited in the quantification of distribution and, more importantly, overlook the potential shift between lookback and horizon windows. To address above challenges, we systematically summarize the distribution shift in TSF into two categories. Regarding lookback windows as input-space and horizon windows as output-space, there exist (i) intra-space shift, that the distribution within the input-space keeps shifted over time, and (ii) inter-space shift, that the distribution is shifted between input-space and output-space. Then we introduce, Dish-TS, a general neural paradigm for alleviating distribution shift in TSF. Specifically, for better distribution estimation, we propose the coefficient net (Conet), which can be any neural architectures, to map input sequences into learnable distribution coefficients. To relieve intra-space and inter-space shift, we organize Dish-TS as a Dual-Conet framework to separately learn the distribution of input- and output-space, which naturally captures the distribution difference of two spaces. In addition, we introduce a more effective training strategy for intractable Conet learning. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on several datasets coupled with different state-of-the-art forecasting models. Experimental results show Dish-TS consistently boosts them with a more than 20% average improvement. In this project, we instead study MoE behavior in an image classification setting, focusing on predictive performance, expert utilization, and generalization. We compare dense, SoftMoE, and SparseMoE classifier heads on the CIFAR10 dataset under comparable model capacity. Both MoE variants achieve slightly higher validation accuracy than the dense baseline while maintaining balanced expert utilization through regularization, avoiding expert collapse. To analyze generalization, we compute Hessian-based sharpness metrics at convergence, including the largest eigenvalue and trace of the loss Hessian, evaluated on both training and test data. We find that SoftMoE exhibits higher sharpness by these metrics, while Dense and SparseMoE lie in a similar curvature regime, despite all models achieving comparable generalization performance. Complementary loss surface perturbation analyses reveal qualitative differences in non-local behavior under finite parameter perturbations between dense and MoE models, which help contextualize curvature-based measurements without directly explaining validation accuracy. A key component of MoEs is the router, which decides which subset of parameters (experts) process which feature embeddings (tokens). In this paper, we present a comprehensive study of routers in MoEs for computer vision tasks. We introduce a unified MoE formulation that subsumes different MoEs with two parametric routing tensors. This formulation covers both sparse MoE, which uses a binary or hard assignment between experts and tokens, and soft MoE, which uses a soft assignment between experts and weighted combinations of tokens. Routers for sparse MoEs can be further grouped into two variants: Token Choice, which matches experts to each token, and Expert Choice, which matches tokens to each expert. We conduct head-to-head experiments with 6 different routers, including existing routers from prior work and new ones we introduce. We show that (i) many routers originally developed for language modeling can be adapted to perform strongly in vision tasks, (ii) in sparse MoE, Expert Choice routers generally outperform Token Choice routers, and (iii) soft MoEs generally outperform sparse MoEs with a fixed compute budget. These results provide new insights regarding the crucial role of routers in vision MoE models.\n\nDeep learning is using ever larger models.       "text": "HI-MoE: Hierarchical Instance-Conditioned\nMixture-of-Experts for Object Detection\nVadim Vashkelis∗ Natalia Trukhina\nAbstract\nMixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable conditional computation by activating only\na subset of model parameters for each input. Although sparse routing has been highly effective\nin language models and has also shown promise in vision, most vision MoE methods operate at\nthe image or patch level. This granularity is poorly aligned with object detection, where the\nfundamental unit of reasoning is an object query corresponding to a candidate instance.\nWe propose Hierarchical Instance-Conditioned Mixture-of-Experts (HI-MoE), a\nDETR-style detection architecture that performs routing in two stages: a lightweight scene\nrouter first selects a scene-consistent expert subset, and an instance router then assigns each\nobject query to a small number of experts within that subset. This design aims to preserve sparse\ncomputation while better matching the heterogeneous, instance-centric structure of detection.\nIn the current draft, experiments are concentrated on COCO with preliminary specialization\nanalysis on LVIS. Under these settings, HI-MoE improves over a dense DINO baseline and\nover simpler token-level or instance-only routing variants, with especially strong gains on small\nobjects. We also provide an initial visualization of expert specialization patterns. We present the\nmethod, ablations, and current limitations in a form intended to support further experimental\nvalidation.\n1 Introduction\nSparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers have become an effective mechanism for scaling neural\nnetworks through conditional computation: instead of activating every parameter for every token,\nthe model learns to select only a small subset of experts [1, 2, 3]. This combination of high parameter\ncapacity and sparse activation has been especially successful in large-scale language models, but\nthe same idea has been less thoroughly explored for vision and, in particular, for object detection.\nVision MoE work such as V-MoE demonstrates that sparse expert routing can improve scaling\nefficiency in transformers by routing image tokens or patches to selected feed-forward experts [4].\nHowever, object detection differs from image classification in a fundamental way: a single image\ncan simultaneously contain tiny, large, rare, occluded, and heavily overlapping instances. These\ncases often demand different processing strategies within the same forward pass.\nDETR-style detectors are a natural setting for conditional expert selection because the decoder\nalready reasons through object queries that correspond to candidate instances [5, 6, 7]. This suggests\nthat routing should occur at the query level rather than only at the image or token level. Intuitively,\na small, ambiguous query in a crowded scene should not have to use the same expert pathway as\nan easy large-object query from the same image.\n∗Corresponding email: research@emilab.org\n1\narXiv:2604.04908v1"
```

```
      "text": "ViMoE: An Empirical Study of Designing Vision Mixture-of-Experts\n\n# ViMoE: An Empirical Study of Designing Vision Mixture-of-Experts\n\nXumeng Han1 Longhui Wei222footnotemark: 2 Zhiyang Dou1 Zipeng Wang1 Chenhui Qiang1 Xin He2 Yingfei Sun1 Zhenjun Han1 Qi Tian2 1 University of Chinese Academic of Sciences 2 Huawei Inc This work was done when Xumeng Han (hanxumeng19@mails.ucas.ac.cn) was an intern at Huawei Inc.Corresponding author: weilh2568@gmail.com, hanzhj@ucas.ac.cn.\n\n###### Abstract\n\nMixture-of-Experts (MoE) models embody the divide-and-conquer concept and are a promising approach for increasing model capacity, demonstrating excellent scalability across multiple domains. In this paper, we integrate the MoE structure into the classic Vision Transformer (ViT), naming it ViMoE, and explore the potential of applying MoE to vision through a comprehensive study on image classification. However, we observe that the performance is sensitive to the configuration of MoE layers, making it challenging to obtain optimal results without careful design. The underlying cause is that inappropriate MoE layers lead to unreliable routing and hinder experts from effectively acquiring helpful knowledge. To address this, we introduce a shared expert to learn and capture common information, serving as an effective way to construct stable ViMoE. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to analyze expert routing behavior, revealing which MoE layers are capable of specializing in handling specific information and which are not. This provides guidance for retaining the critical layers while removing redundancies, thereby advancing ViMoE to be more efficient without sacrificing accuracy. We aspire for this work to offer new insights into the design of vision MoE models and provide valuable empirical guidance for future research.\n\n## 1 Introduction\n\nFigure 1: Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K. We compare ViMoE with other ViT architecture baselines. However, larger models require significant computational resources for training and deployment, and balancing performance with efficiency remains a critical issue, especially in resource-constrained environments. A promising approach is to use the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) (Jacobs et al., 1991; Eigen et al., 2013) layers in neural networks, which decouple model size from inference efficiency. MoE embodies the divide-and-conquer principle, where feature embeddings are routed to selected experts through a gating mechanism, allowing each expert to specialize in a subsets of the data. ## Novelty Assessment — Findings
```

I ran 6 targeted Exa searches across MoE routing collapse, normalization-induced information loss, time series MoE, vision MoE, parameter-efficient routing, and information-bottleneck normalization. Reviewed 50+ candidate papers. **The specific principle is not identified in prior work.** Here's the careful breakdown.

### Closest theoretical analogue (uncited, should add)

**Wang, Hayou, Nalisnick — "The Myth of Expert Specialization in MoEs" (arXiv:2604.09780, April 2026, Johns Hopkins)** — This is the most theoretically adjacent contemporaneous work. They prove:
- "MoE routers are linear maps, hidden state similarity is both necessary and sufficient to explain expert usage similarity"
- "load-balancing loss suppresses shared hidden state directions to maintain routing diversity, which might provide a theoretical explanation for specialization collapse under less diverse data"

**Differentiation:** They identify that routing reflects *hidden state geometry*. They do not identify *what shapes that geometry*. Your paper traces the geometry back to instance normalization as the upstream cause. They stop one step before your diagnosis. This is a citable companion result, not a scoop.

### Conceptually adjacent (uncited, should add)

**Zou et al. — "IBNorm: Information-Bottleneck Inspired Normalization" (arXiv:2510.25262, Oct 2025, Singapore Management University)** — argues existing normalizations are "variance-centric": "two representations may share identical mean and variance, but can encode drastically different amounts of task-relevant information." Conceptually similar (normalization removes task-relevant info), but: (a) targets representation learning quality, not routing; (b) doesn't connect to MoE; (c) generic deep learning, not instance-level normalization on time series.

### Adjacent but already cited or different mechanism

| Paper | What they show | Why it's not your finding |
|---|---|---|
| Mohamud et al. 2026 (arXiv:2604.00421) "Self-Routing" | Hidden-state subspace as expert logits | Doesn't claim normalization is the bottleneck; routes on hidden states (which your paper shows fail) |
| Chi et al. NeurIPS 2022 "Representation Collapse of Sparse MoE" | Token clustering around expert centroids → hyperspherical routing | Different cause (training dynamics from routing itself), not normalization |
| Symbiotic-MoE (arXiv:2604.07753) | Routing collapse from gradient conflicts in multimodal MoE | Different cause (cross-modality task interference) |
| Fu & Yang (arXiv:2510.04667) "Noise or Signal?" RevIN failures | RevIN catastrophically fails on outliers (+683% MSE) | Different failure mode (outlier sensitivity), not routing |
| Berthelier 2026 (arXiv:2603.11869) | RevIN components redundant/detrimental | Already cited; doesn't connect to MoE |
| DishTS (Fan et al. AAAI 2023) | Re-injects per-window statistics for non-stationarity | Already cited; for forecasting accuracy, not routing |
| MoE-F, GateTS, MFMformer, N-BEATS-MoE, GMM-TS, CrossSparse-MoE | Time-series MoE architectures | None diagnose routing collapse from normalization |
| ViMoE, V-MoE, Routers in Vision MoE empirical study, HI-MoE, SERA | Vision MoE design and routing | None identify InstanceNorm-induced collapse |

### Verdict

**The principle holds as novel.** No prior work identifies *normalization-induced routing collapse* — that instance-level normalization destroys routing information by stripping per-window statistics that carry the routing signal — let alone validates it cross-modality on ViT.

The cross-modality result (ViT + InstanceNorm1d → collapse) is also unprecedented in the vision MoE literature.

### Recommended additions to Related Work

Two concrete edits worth making to harden the novelty claim against reviewers who will run the same searches:

1. **Add Wang, Hayou, Nalisnick 2026** to the "MoE routing collapse and rescue" paragraph (line 85), with explicit differentiation:

   > "Concurrently, Wang et al. (2026) prove MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry — tokens with similar hidden states activate similar experts. We extend this one step upstream: we identify what *shapes* that geometry on TSFMs. Instance normalization homogenizes hidden states by stripping per-window statistics, producing the geometric collapse Wang et al. analyze."

2. **Add IBNorm (Zou et al. 2025)** to the "Normalization in Time Series" paragraph (line 99), with differentiation:

   > "Concurrent work (Zou et al., 2025) argues variance-centric normalization (BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm) is suboptimal for representation learning because two representations with identical mean and variance can encode different amounts of task-relevant information. We identify a specific, mechanistic consequence: when the stripped statistics carry the *routing* signal in a downstream MoE, normalization causes catastrophic collapse."

These additions both demonstrate awareness of the latest literature and pre-empt reviewer objections about overlapping work. Want me to make these edits?

```
85	\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Routing collapse---where a few experts capture all traffic---is a well-known failure mode in MoE training. Existing solutions attack it from the \emph{optimization side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, Expert-Choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}, and ReLU gating~\citep{zhang2025remoe}. AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} brings MoE to adapter fine-tuning in NLP but still routes on hidden states. All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's \emph{input} contains discriminative information in the first place. We sweep all five families across eleven configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN and show \textbf{none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA} (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Our contribution is complementary: we show that when normalization structurally removes routing information from hidden states, no configuration from any of the five standard rescue families can compensate. Concurrently, recent work in NLP and vision has moved toward eliminating external routers entirely: AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} lets experts self-select via activation norms, ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} routes via cosine similarity to learned eigenbases (achieving 0\% collapse), and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} encapsulates gating within each expert. We validate this self-routing principle in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}): self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses---confirming the bottleneck is normalization, not router design.
86	
87	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Normalization in Time Series.} RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} mitigates distribution shift; DishTS~\citep{fan2023dishts} and Non-stationary Transformers~\citep{liu2022nonstationary} partially recover stripped statistics. Concurrently, \citet{berthelier2026revin} independently show that several RevIN components are redundant or detrimental. We identify a consequence not previously characterized in the MoE literature: RevIN strips the per-window statistics that substantially aid discriminative gating in MoE routers.}
88	
89	\textbf{NAS and LLM-Guided Search.} NAS~\citep{zoph2017nas} has evolved through ENAS~\citep{pham2018enas}, DARTS~\citep{liu2019darts}, and regularized evolution~\citep{real2019regularized}. Shears~\citep{munoz2024shears} and RZ-NAS~\citep{ji2025rznas} search adapter hyperparameters for LLMs; NAS-LoRA~\citep{chen2025naslora} targets vision adapters. FunSearch~\citep{romera2024funsearch}, EvoPrompting~\citep{chen2023evoprompting}, PartEvo~\citep{hu2025partevo}, and ReEvo~\citep{ye2024reevo} demonstrate LLM-guided program synthesis. We use this paradigm for expert pool construction (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}).
```

```
65:\textbf{Why keep the backbone frozen?} Frozen-backbone adaptation enables deployment regimes that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot serve. A single TSFM in GPU VRAM serves thousands of tenants via 426K-parameter adapters (${\sim}1.7$\,MB each) swapped in microseconds---eliminating $O(N)$ independent training pipelines. On-device deployment and cross-task reuse impose similar constraints (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}). As TSFMs scale toward billion-parameter regimes~\citep{shi2024timemoe}, frozen-backbone PEFT becomes an increasingly important per-dataset adaptation path.
585:\textbf{Practitioner guideline.} Before deploying MoE adapters on TSFMs with instance normalization, compute $R(\mathcal{D})$: in our experiments, values above $0.5$ predict raw routing helps; below $0.2$, it does not (validated on 9 LTSF datasets). \textbf{Limitations:} Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} is untested; Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} covers linear backbones only (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory} confirms the mechanism in full Transformers); $R(\mathcal{D})$ uses first moments and may miss higher-order routing signals (Solar outlier).
1672:\caption{\textbf{DLinear supervised calibration} (trained from scratch, no backbone, 3 seeds, test MSE mean$\pm$std). The gap to RR-MoA is expected; the frozen-backbone paradigm is motivated by deployment constraints (\S\ref{sec:intro}).}
1824:The frozen-backbone paradigm is motivated by three deployment regimes where full fine-tuning is infeasible:
1826:\textbf{(i) Multi-tenant cloud serving.} A single TSFM sits in GPU VRAM and serves thousands of tenants via lightweight, hot-swappable per-tenant adapters in host RAM. Per-tenant DLinear requires collecting, storing, and periodically retraining on each tenant's historical data ($O(N)$ training pipelines for $N$ tenants), whereas the frozen backbone is loaded once and adapter weights (${\sim}50$--$500$K parameters, ${\sim}0.2$--$2$\,MB) are swapped from host RAM in microseconds. At $N{=}1{,}000$ tenants, the adapter approach eliminates $1{,}000$ independent training jobs and enables instant onboarding of new tenants via zero-shot transfer---capabilities absent from per-tenant supervised baselines.
```

```
55:Time series foundation models (TSFMs) like MOMENT and Moirai provide powerful pretrained representations, but adapting them to a downstream task requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions. Standard TSFM benchmarks use a single static head---one adapter topology for every input window. A natural improvement is a mixture-of-expert (MoE) adapter, where a router selects the best expert head for each window. However, on TSFMs with instance normalization, this \textbf{catastrophically fails}: the router learns to send \emph{every} window to the \emph{same} expert---routing entropy collapses to $0.000{\pm}0.000$, and the remaining experts are never used. We identify \textbf{normalization-induced routing collapse}: instance normalization strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish input regimes, leaving it with homogenized hidden states that all look alike. Eight converging causal controls isolate the mechanism---most strikingly, opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Timer-XL rises $1.49{\to}1.60$ while MOMENT collapses $0.60{\to}0.00$)---and all five standard MoE-rescue families (load balancing, z-loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, expert-choice) across eleven configurations fail ($2.7{\times}$ worse; 720 runs). A mutual-information decomposition formalizes the mechanism and yields a signal-ratio predictor ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$) that identifies where collapse occurs, including boundary cases where it does \emph{not} (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix principle is clear: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$) on the primary backbone and generalizing across four additional backbones (two negative controls without instance normalization confirm specificity). A predicted consequence---the \textbf{Frozen Paradox}---is confirmed: frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$, because unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse. An extension restoring raw-signal access to experts matches or beats DLinear on 6/6 datasets (Appendix).
73:\textbf{(1)~A principle validated across three normalization families and two modalities: instance normalization destroys routing information when the stripped statistics carry the routing signal.} A mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) shows that instance normalization destroys routing MI by exactly the information in the stripped location-scale statistics. The principle makes four \textbf{testable predictions}, all confirmed: (a)~$R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts which datasets benefit ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}); (b)~backbones without instance normalization should not collapse (Timer-XL, Chronos; \S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}); (c)~cross-modality transfer (ViT$+$InstanceNorm1d collapses; ResNet does not; Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}); (d)~a phase-transition threshold $\alpha^* {=} R/(R{+}1) {\approx} 0.40$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:phase_transition}, Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}). Eight converging causal controls isolate the mechanism, the most striking being opposite entropy trajectories: MOMENT collapses ($0.60{\to}0.00$) while Timer-XL \emph{rises} ($1.49{\to}1.60$)---same code, same data, only the normalization differs.
356:In contrast, \textbf{RR-MoA} maintains healthy routing entropy ($1.0$--$1.57$) and wins \textbf{54/54} configurations, with MSE improvements of $27\%$ to $77\%$ over the best fixed adapter. Notably, on Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, where the stripped statistics carry little information), RR-MoA does not improve over fixed adapters---exactly as Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}).
417:{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Rawness vs.\ bypass and dose-response.} Replacing the router's raw input with RevIN-normalized input degrades MSE by $60$--$88\%$ while entropy stays high (Table~\ref{tab:router_input}, Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}), confirming the router relies on the \emph{content} of the stripped statistics, not merely the bypass path. A dose-response interpolation $\mathbf{x}_\alpha = (1{-}\alpha)\,\mathbf{x}_\text{raw} + \alpha\,\text{RevIN}(\mathbf{x}_\text{raw})$ reveals a \emph{phase transition} (Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}; 150 runs): MSE degrades mildly for $\alpha{\leq}0.75$ ($+5.4\%$) but catastrophically at $\alpha{=}1.0$ ($+283\%$), while entropy stays in $[1.43, 1.57]$---normalization renders routing uninformative without reducing diversity. The phase transition threshold is quantitatively predicted at $\alpha^* = R(\mathcal{D})/(R(\mathcal{D})+1) \approx 0.40$ for the median benchmark (Appendix~\ref{app:prop2_depth}). A temporal-shuffle ablation confirms routing depends on $(M,\Sigma)$ statistics, not temporal ordering (Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}).}
491:    \item[\textup{(iv)}] \textbf{Signal ratio as sufficient-statistic proxy.} Since Part~(iii) establishes that $(M,\Sigma)$ are sufficient statistics for $E$ when the router depends entirely on them, the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ measures the variance contribution of these sufficient statistics relative to the residual shape---a monotone proxy for the \emph{potential} routing information in the stripped statistics. The leakage $\varepsilon$ varies by dataset ($0.09$--$1.26$ nats via CCA; cross-validated within ${\pm}0.2$ nats by the KSG estimator~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}); $R(\mathcal{D})$ is validated at $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ across nine datasets. \textbf{Tightness:} direct measurement of $H(E \mid S)$ via held-out classifier confirms normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of routing entropy; the bound~(ii) gap averages $0.075$ nats ($4.7\%$ of $\log K$; Appendix~\ref{app:mi_tightness}).\footnote{$H(E \mid S)$ does not correlate with $\Delta\%$ ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$); $R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts improvement because it measures routing \emph{potential}, not the MI loss itself.}
497:\textbf{Quantitative prediction.} The \emph{routing signal ratio} $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\text{Var}(M) + \text{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\text{Var}(S)}$ measures whether input windows in a dataset differ primarily in their location and scale (high $R$, normalization destroys the dominant routing signal) or primarily in their shape (low $R$, routing signal survives normalization). It serves as a monotone proxy for the MI bound. Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio} validates this: the Spearman rank correlation between $R(\mathcal{D})$ and the MSE improvement $\Delta\%$ from raw routing is $\rho = -0.88$ ($p < 0.002$; bootstrap CI: $[-1.00, -0.51]$; $n{=}9$), i.e., datasets where normalization strips more routing signal benefit more from bypassing it. Traffic ($R{=}0.14$) is correctly predicted as a boundary case ($\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$). Solar ($R{=}0.06$) is the one outlier: the Conv1d router exploits temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale, consistent with the SSR ablation ($+43\%$ degradation). Additional ablations (SSR, RDGF, per-quartile analysis) in Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}.
540:    xlabel={Signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D})$},
568:\label{fig:signal_ratio}
585:\textbf{Practitioner guideline.} Before deploying MoE adapters on TSFMs with instance normalization, compute $R(\mathcal{D})$: in our experiments, values above $0.5$ predict raw routing helps; below $0.2$, it does not (validated on 9 LTSF datasets). \textbf{Limitations:} Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} is untested; Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} covers linear backbones only (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory} confirms the mechanism in full Transformers); $R(\mathcal{D})$ uses first moments and may miss higher-order routing signals (Solar outlier).
986:\emph{Tightness condition.} The bound~(ii) is informative when $I(M,\Sigma; E) \gg \varepsilon$. Since $I(M,\Sigma; E)$ increases with the location-scale variance, the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ is a monotone proxy for the tightness of the bound. This explains the $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ correlation: high-$R$ datasets (Exchange, $R{=}2.17$) have $I(M,\Sigma; E) \gg \varepsilon$, producing large gains ($-68.5\%$); low-$R$ datasets (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$) have $I(M,\Sigma; E) \approx \varepsilon$, producing no gain ($+2.9\%$).
996:\textbf{Rate-distortion interpretation of $R(\mathcal{D})$.}
997:Instance normalization is a \emph{deterministic lossy compression}: it maps $X \mapsto S$, discarding $(M, \Sigma)$. In rate-distortion theory~\citep{cover2006elements}, this compression has rate $R_\text{strip} = I(X; M, \Sigma \mid S)$ and distortion (for routing) $D_\text{route} = H(E \mid S) - H(E \mid X) = I(M, \Sigma; E \mid S)$, which is exactly Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i). Under Gaussianity, the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D})$ is proportional to the rate-distortion slope at the normalization operating point: it measures how much routing capacity is consumed by the statistics that normalization strips. Specifically, if the joint $(M, \Sigma, S)$ is multivariate Gaussian, then $I(M, \Sigma; E) \propto \log(1 + R(\mathcal{D}))$ (by the Gaussian mutual information formula), making $R(\mathcal{D})$ a \emph{monotone surrogate for the bits lost to normalization}. The validated $\rho = -0.88$ correlation (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}) is thus not a statistical coincidence but a consequence of this rate-distortion structure.
1007:    \alpha^* \;\approx\; \frac{R(\mathcal{D})}{R(\mathcal{D}) + 1}
1012:\emph{Validation.} For the median $R(\mathcal{D}) = 0.67$ across our benchmarks, Proposition~\ref{prop:phase_transition} predicts $\alpha^* \approx 0.40$. The dose-response experiment (Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}; 150 runs) confirms this: MSE degrades mildly for $\alpha \leq 0.75$ ($+5.4\%$) but catastrophically at $\alpha = 1.0$ ($+283\%$). The sharpness of the transition arises from the softmax: when $P_\mathrm{route}(\alpha) / P_\mathrm{noise}$ drops below ${\sim}1$, routing weights converge to uniform regardless of expert relevance.
1504:\textbf{ResNet-18: normalization prevents collapse.} Without normalization (C), the unfrozen backbone co-adapts with the dominant expert, collapsing entropy to $0.184\pm0.260$---confirming Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}. Adding InstanceNorm2d (A) or BatchNorm2d (D) \emph{prevents} collapse ($1.48\pm0.02$), the \emph{opposite} of time series. Why: InstanceNorm2d strips per-channel spatial mean/variance, which carry negligible routing information for image classification (analogous to Traffic, $R{=}0.14$).
```

## Verification Results

### Claim 1: "values above 0.5 predict raw routing helps, below 0.2 it does not"

The actual data (Figure `fig:signal_ratio`, line 549):

| Dataset | R(D) | Δ% | Helps? |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Solar | 0.06 | **−32.9%** | YES (outlier — paper flags this) |
| Traffic | 0.14 | +2.9% | NO ✓ |
| Electricity | 0.24 | −26.8% | YES (between 0.2–0.5) |
| ETTh1 | 0.57 | −43.2% | YES ✓ |
| ETTm1 | 0.67 | −51.1% | YES ✓ |
| Weather | 0.70 | −44.6% | YES ✓ |
| ETTh2 | 1.16 | −71.0% | YES ✓ |
| ETTm2 | 1.24 | −77.2% | YES ✓ |
| Exchange | 2.17 | −66.5% | YES ✓ |

**The "below 0.2 it does not help" threshold is undermined by Solar (R=0.06, Δ=−32.9%).** The paper itself flags Solar as "the one outlier" at line 506 because the Conv1d router exploits temporal patterns beyond location-scale. But the practitioner guideline at line 585 doesn't acknowledge this caveat — a reviewer comparing the guideline to the data would catch the contradiction. Also: only 2 data points fall below 0.2 (Solar + Traffic), and 1 of them violates the threshold. n=2 is thin.

The "above 0.5 helps" threshold is solid: all 6 datasets above 0.5 help substantially.

### Claim 2: Multi-tenant deployment as paper contribution

You're right. Frozen-backbone multi-tenant adapter deployment is a known benefit of PEFT (LoRA, Houlsby 2019, etc.), not a contribution of this paper. The current framing in slides line 60 reads like a contribution claim. The paper line 65 is borderline acceptable because it says frozen-backbone "adaptation enables" (not "we enable") — but the slides version is stronger and could be misread as ownership.

### Recommended edits

**For claim 1** — soften the practitioner guideline to acknowledge Solar:

> "Practitioner guideline. Compute $R(\mathcal{D})$: in our 9 LTSF benchmarks, values above 0.5 reliably predict raw routing helps (6/6 datasets, 27–77% improvement). Below 0.2 the prediction is less reliable: Traffic (R=0.14) is correctly predicted to not benefit, but Solar (R=0.06) does benefit because the Conv1d router exploits temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale (SSR ablation, Appendix `app:routing_ablations`). For low-R datasets, the signal ratio captures necessary but not sufficient conditions."

```
65:\textbf{Why keep the backbone frozen?} Frozen-backbone adaptation is compatible with established multi-tenant adapter deployment regimes~\citep{houlsby2019adapters,hu2022lora}---regimes that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot serve. A single TSFM in GPU VRAM can serve thousands of tenants via 426K-parameter adapters (${\sim}1.7$\,MB each) swapped in microseconds---eliminating $O(N)$ independent training pipelines. On-device deployment and cross-task reuse impose similar constraints (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}). As TSFMs scale toward billion-parameter regimes~\citep{shi2024timemoe}, frozen-backbone PEFT becomes an increasingly important per-dataset adaptation path.
81:\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard approach to adapting a frozen TSFM is to attach a lightweight module---LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}---and tune it on downstream data. Recent work has expanded the design space: MSFT~\citep{qiao2025msft} proposes multi-scale finetuning, TRACE~\citep{li2025trace} introduces importance-based LoRA selection with reconstructed heads, and AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} adapts input representations rather than the backbone itself. Beyond LoRA~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora} surveys PEFT alternatives for Chronos; Prune-then-Finetune~\citep{zhao2025prune} applies structured pruning; in-context fine-tuning~\citep{faw2025icf} adapts at inference time. TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval} address model selection and benchmarking. All of these search over finetuning \textit{strategies}---learning rates, rank, which layers to tune---rather than the adapter \textit{architecture} itself. Our work addresses this gap: we show that the choice of adapter topology should be \emph{per-sample}, not per-dataset.
686:\bibitem[Hu and Wallis(2022)]{hu2022lora}
691:\bibitem[Houlsby et~al.(2019)]{houlsby2019adapters}
```

> DEVELOPER

what does this one really mean: "the Frozen Paradox proposition covers linear backbones only (though confirmed empirically on full Transformers), "

> AGENT

This is a hedge about the **scope of the formal mathematical proof** vs the **scope of the empirical evidence**.

**What "linear backbones only" means:**

Proposition 2 (`prop:frozen` at line 282 of the paper) proves the gradient co-adaptation collapse mechanism for a *toy mathematical model*:

> "Consider a 2-expert MoE with backbone $\mathbf{h} = A\mathbf{x}$, router $p = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{h})$, loss $\ell = p\,\ell_1 + (1-p)\,\ell_2$. Under gradient descent on $(A, \mathbf{w})$..."

The backbone is a **single linear matrix** $A$. No nonlinearities, no attention, no LayerNorm, no skip connections — just $\mathbf{h} = A\mathbf{x}$ followed by a sigmoid router. Two experts. The math of the proof relies on this simple structure to derive the closed-form result that $\dot{\ell}_k \propto -p_k \|\nabla_\mathbf{h} \ell_k\|^2$, which causes the dominant expert's loss to decrease faster, creating self-reinforcing collapse toward $p \in \{0, 1\}$.

**Why this is a limitation:**

Real TSFM backbones (MOMENT-small) are **8-layer Transformers** with multi-head self-attention, LayerNorm, residual connections, FFN blocks, RevIN, and patch tokenization. The proof does NOT prove that the same collapse mechanism mathematically holds in this much more complex architecture. A reviewer could ask: "Your toy proof is for linear $A\mathbf{x}$ — how do you know it generalizes to deep nonlinear Transformers?"

**Why "confirmed empirically on full Transformers" closes the gap:**

Figure 1b (the trajectory figure, `fig:trajectory`) measures the actual entropy collapse trajectory on the real 8-block MOMENT Transformer with all its complexity, and shows entropy crashes from 0.5 to 0.000 in ~50 training steps. So the *prediction* of the simple proof — collapse via gradient feedback loop — is empirically observed in the full architecture, even though the *math* only formally covers the toy linear case.

**The honest reading:** "We have a clean mathematical proof for a simplified model that captures the essential mechanism, and we verify by direct measurement that the same collapse pattern occurs in the real deep Transformer the paper actually studies." This is a standard limitation pattern in ML theory — proofs tend to be tractable only for simplified models, with empirical validation closing the gap. A reviewer might still push for a stronger theorem, but this hedging is appropriate and honest.

The line in the conclusion is just calling this out explicitly so reviewers don't accuse the paper of overclaiming the theory.

> AGENT

No — they are **two distinct architectures targeting two different problems**, though both follow the same principle of "give the architecture access to the raw input somewhere."

| | SR-MoA | Residual-IA⁺ (dual-stream) |
|---|---|---|
| **What it fixes** | The *router* | The *experts* |
| **Where raw input enters** | Per-expert sigmoid *gate* (decides whether expert fires) | Per-expert *output stream* (a shared NLinear branch on raw input is added to every expert's output) |
| **Per-expert formula** | $\mathbf{y}_k = \sigma(W_k \cdot \mathbf{X}_\text{raw}) \cdot \text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$ | $\mathbf{y}_k = \text{NLinear}(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}) + \sigma(\text{blend}_k(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})) \cdot \text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$ |
| **Has external router?** | No (replaces RR-MoA's Conv1d router with self-gating) | Yes (still uses self-gating like SR-MoA, or RR-MoA's Conv1d, both work) |
| **What it proves** | **Architecture-agnostic principle**: routing on raw input works regardless of router design (external Conv1d vs per-expert self-gating). The bottleneck is the input, not the router. | **Diagnosis is actionable**: RevIN strips forecasting signal too (not just routing signal), so giving experts a raw-input branch closes the DLinear gap. |
| **Result** | Outperforms RR-MoA by 13–42% across 6 datasets (252 runs) | Matches/beats DLinear on 6/6 at H=96; 107/123 cells across full grid |
| **Relationship to RR-MoA** | A **router replacement** (different architecture, same principle) | A **per-expert extension** that can be stacked on RR-MoA *or* SR-MoA |

**They can be combined.** The paper introduces **SR-RIA⁺** (line 2196) as the combination — SR-MoA's self-routing + Residual-IA⁺'s dual-stream experts. That confirms they're orthogonal contributions: one fixes routing, the other fixes expert information access.

**The conceptual link:** Both follow the same diagnostic logic — "RevIN destroys information; restore raw-input access." But they restore it at different points: SR-MoA at the gate, Residual-IA⁺ at the expert output. So they're independent validations of the same diagnosis from different architectural angles.

**Why this matters for the paper's logic:** SR-MoA validates that routing is the *principle*, not the specific router design (Section 4 main result). Residual-IA⁺ validates that the diagnosis is *actionable* by closing the gap to a from-scratch supervised baseline (Section 4 + Appendix). Together they form two independent lines of evidence that "instance normalization destroys information that experts need" is the right diagnosis.

> AGENT

Yes — three architectural proposals, plus one combination. Here's the full inventory:

| # | Name | What it does | Status in the paper |
|---|------|------|---|
| 1 | **RR-MoA** (Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters) | External Conv1d gate reads raw input → Top-K routing across K=5 expert heads, all of which read hidden states only | **Headline contribution.** The minimal instantiation of the "route on raw input" principle. 54/54 wins. |
| 2 | **SR-MoA** (Self-Routed MoA) | No external router. Each expert has its own sigmoid gate on raw input: $\mathbf{y}_k = \sigma_k(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}) \cdot \text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$ | **Architecture-agnostic validation.** Proves the principle is the *raw input*, not the router design. Outperforms RR-MoA by 13–42%. |
| 3 | **Residual-IA⁺** (Dual-stream extension) | External router (any of the above), but each expert combines a shared raw-input NLinear branch with a gated backbone residual: $\mathbf{y}_k = \text{NLinear}(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}) + \sigma(\text{blend}_k) \cdot \text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$ | **Diagnosis-actionability proof.** Closes the gap to DLinear by giving experts (not just the router) raw-input access. 107/123 match-or-beat. |
| 4 | **SR-RIA⁺** (combination) | SR-MoA self-routing + Residual-IA⁺ dual-stream experts stacked together | Appendix-only combination, mentioned at line 2196. Confirms the two extensions are orthogonal. |

**The narrative arc the paper builds:**

1. **RR-MoA** is the headline — minimal fix derived directly from the diagnosis.
2. **SR-MoA** answers "is it the principle or the architecture?" — different router design, same raw-input principle, even better results.
3. **Residual-IA⁺** answers "is the diagnosis actionable beyond just routing?" — yes, restoring raw access at the expert level closes the DLinear gap.
4. **SR-RIA⁺** confirms 2 and 3 are independent and stack — the principle works at any point you restore raw-input access.

**Why three (not one) matters for reviewers:** A single architecture's success could be attributed to that specific design. Three independent architectures all confirming the same diagnosis (route/access raw input) makes it much harder to dismiss as architectural luck. This is the paper's "principle, not method" framing — RR-MoA is just the cleanest instantiation, not the only one.

**Naming watch-out:** Make sure the slides and abstract are consistent about which is which. The abstract currently centers on RR-MoA (correct — it's the headline). SR-MoA appears in §4 architecture-agnostic discussion. Residual-IA⁺ appears in the appendix gap-closing section. If any slide accidentally uses the names interchangeably, that's a clarity bug worth fixing.

```
55:Time series foundation models (TSFMs) like MOMENT and Moirai provide powerful pretrained representations, but adapting them to a downstream task requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions. Standard TSFM benchmarks use a single static head---one adapter topology for every input window. A natural improvement is a mixture-of-expert (MoE) adapter, where a router selects the best expert head for each window. However, on TSFMs with instance normalization, this \textbf{catastrophically fails}: the router learns to send \emph{every} window to the \emph{same} expert---routing entropy collapses to $0.000{\pm}0.000$, and the remaining experts are never used. We identify \textbf{normalization-induced routing collapse}: instance normalization strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish input regimes, leaving it with homogenized hidden states that all look alike. Eight converging causal controls isolate the mechanism---most strikingly, opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Timer-XL rises $1.49{\to}1.60$ while MOMENT collapses $0.60{\to}0.00$)---and all five standard MoE-rescue families (load balancing, z-loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, expert-choice) across eleven configurations fail ($2.7{\times}$ worse; 720 runs). A mutual-information decomposition formalizes the mechanism and yields a signal-ratio predictor ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$) that identifies where collapse occurs, including boundary cases where it does \emph{not} (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix principle is clear: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$) on the primary backbone and generalizing across four additional backbones (two negative controls without instance normalization confirm specificity). A predicted consequence---the \textbf{Frozen Paradox}---is confirmed: frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$, because unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse. An extension restoring raw-signal access to experts matches or beats DLinear on 6/6 datasets (Appendix).
69:\textbf{Our fix.} Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix principle is clear: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on the raw, pre-normalization input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ while keeping the backbone strictly frozen. Only the router and five canonical expert heads are trainable. Eleven standard MoE-rescue mechanisms (load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss, ReLU routing, expert-choice) all fail to recover performance ($2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA across 720 runs; Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), confirming that the problem is in the router's \emph{input}, not its \emph{optimization}.
75:\textbf{(2)~Fix and a predicted consequence.} Because the principle pinpoints the cause, the fix follows directly: RR-MoA routes on raw pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}). The principle also predicts a \textbf{Frozen Paradox}: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}), so frozen adapters should beat full fine-tuning---confirmed at $12$--$79\%$ across all six datasets. RR-MoA generalizes across four RevIN/LayerNorm backbones; two negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL) confirm instance-normalization-specificity.
83:\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been applied \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale model capacity: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes frequency bands across internal experts, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. These designs place experts inside the backbone architecture. RR-MoA instead applies MoE at the \emph{adapter level} on a frozen backbone---an orthogonal design axis. We validate that the two axes stack: RR-MoA on top of Moirai-MoE still yields $-37\%$ MSE (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).
85:\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Routing collapse---where a few experts capture all traffic---is a well-known failure mode in MoE training. Existing solutions attack it from the \emph{optimization side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, Expert-Choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}, and ReLU gating~\citep{zhang2025remoe}. AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} brings MoE to adapter fine-tuning in NLP but still routes on hidden states. All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's \emph{input} contains discriminative information in the first place. We sweep all five families across eleven configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN and show \textbf{none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA} (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Our contribution is complementary: we show that when normalization structurally removes routing information from hidden states, no configuration from any of the five standard rescue families can compensate. Concurrently, recent work in NLP and vision has moved toward eliminating external routers entirely: AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} lets experts self-select via activation norms, ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} routes via cosine similarity to learned eigenbases (achieving 0\% collapse), and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} encapsulates gating within each expert. We validate this self-routing principle in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}): self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses---confirming the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Concurrent theoretical work~\citep{wang2026myth} proves MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry: tokens with similar hidden states activate similar experts. We extend this one step upstream by identifying what \emph{shapes} that geometry on TSFMs---instance normalization homogenizes hidden states by stripping per-window statistics, producing the geometric collapse that geometry-based analyses describe but do not causally explain.
205:\caption{\textbf{RR-MoA architecture.} \textit{Path~A} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf{H}$ (no gradients through $\theta$); all experts receive $\mathbf{H}$. \textit{Path~B} (orange): a lightweight Conv1d gate (1{,}100 params) reads the raw pre-normalization signal $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ and selects the Top-2 experts via sparse routing. Only the selected experts (bold) contribute to the output; inactive experts (gray) receive no gradient. Standard MoE routing on $\mathbf{H}$ collapses (entropy $0.000{\pm}0.000$; Table~\ref{tab:adamix}); RR-MoA achieves \textbf{54/54 wins} (Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa}).}
217:\subsection{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)}
220:The goal of per-window routing is to select, for each input window, the subset of expert adapters best suited to that window's characteristics---so that a quiet baseline and a volatile spike are handled by different adapter topologies rather than forced through the same head. As shown in the introduction, this fails when the router reads normalized hidden states, because RevIN removes the per-window statistics that distinguish input regimes. \textbf{RR-MoA} avoids this by splitting the information into two streams: the frozen TSFM produces deep embeddings $\mathbf{H}$ for the experts, while a separate lightweight gate reads the \textit{raw, pre-normalization} input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ to decide which experts to activate:
230:\caption{RR-MoA: Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters with Top-$k$ sparse routing}
250:We evaluate RR-MoA on standard long-term forecasting benchmarks using five backbones, seven baselines, and up to five random seeds per configuration.
262:\subsection{RR-MoA: Routing Collapse and Its Resolution}
267:This section proceeds in four steps: we first show that RR-MoA consistently outperforms fixed adapters (Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa}), then diagnose why standard MoE routing fails (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}), demonstrate that no standard rescue mechanism recovers performance (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), and finally compare against a comprehensive baseline suite (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).
269:{\looseness=-1 \textbf{RR-MoA vs.\ fixed adapters.} Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa} compares Top-2 RR-MoA against the best fixed adapter, using the \emph{same five expert heads} in all rows. Across 6 datasets $\times$ 3 freeze levels $\times$ 3 seeds $=$ \textbf{54 configurations}, RR-MoA wins every one with tight standard deviations.}
273:\caption{\textbf{Freeze-level ablation} (test MSE, mean$\pm$std, 3 seeds, H=96). RR-MoA (Top-2, same 5 experts) vs.\ best of $\{$linear, attention, conv$\}$. RR-MoA wins \textbf{54/54} across 6 datasets (extended grid in Appendix~\ref{app:extended_rrmoa}); improvement is largest when frozen (``Frozen Paradox'').}
278:Dataset & Freeze level & RR-MoA (Top-2) & Best fixed & $\Delta$\% \\
298:{\looseness=-1 \textbf{The Frozen Paradox.} Frozen RR-MoA beats \emph{full fine-tuning} (all 8 blocks unfrozen, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs) by $12$--$79\%$ on every dataset (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}, Figure~\ref{fig:frozen_paradox}). Two distinct mechanisms contribute. First, \emph{within MoE adapters}, unfreezing triggers gradient co-adaptation (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}): the dominant expert reshapes the shared backbone, collapsing routing---freezing prevents this loop and preserves expert diversity. Second, \emph{across architectures}, the frozen five-expert mixture with learned per-sample routing provides an architectural advantage that a single unfrozen head cannot match even with full parameter access: per-sample expert selection captures input-regime structure that no single topology can represent. Within RR-MoA, frozen is best on 4/6 datasets; light unfreezing wins by up to $13\%$ on the other two. SR-MoA independently replicates this pattern (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). Even with careful hyperparameter tuning---learning rates $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-6}$, 100 epochs, cosine schedule with 10-epoch warmup, layerwise LR decay, weight decay sweep, gradient accumulation up to effective batch 512 (90 configurations)---full fine-tuning still loses by $51$--$71\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_ft}).}
337:{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Why does standard MoE routing fail?} To understand the source of RR-MoA's advantage, we examine AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix}, which uses the standard recipe of routing on hidden states. Table~\ref{tab:adamix} shows that AdaMix collapses to a single expert whenever backbone layers are unfrozen: entropy reaches $0.000\pm0.000$ in 7/12 unfrozen configurations; the remaining 5 stay below $0.55$ (vs.\ max ${\approx}1.61$) with high cross-seed variance ($\sigma$ up to $0.71$), indicating stochastic collapse rather than stable partial routing. The green rows reveal the cause: disabling RevIN inside MOMENT recovers entropy from $0.000$ to $0.66$--$1.32$, proving that normalization is the causal mechanism (BatchNorm1d and GroupNorm produce the same collapse; Appendix~\ref{app:norm_generalization}). The causal contrast is sharpest when comparing backbones directly (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast}): under identical last-4 unfreezing on identical data, MOMENT entropy crashes to $0.000$ in ${\sim}40$ steps while Timer-XL (which lacks RevIN) stays at $1.60$ for all $400$ steps---opposite trajectories from the same code.}
356:In contrast, \textbf{RR-MoA} maintains healthy routing entropy ($1.0$--$1.57$) and wins \textbf{54/54} configurations, with MSE improvements of $27\%$ to $77\%$ over the best fixed adapter. Notably, on Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, where the stripped statistics carry little information), RR-MoA does not improve over fixed adapters---exactly as Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}).
358:\textbf{Rescue-baseline sweep.} To rule out that the collapse is merely under-tuned, we sweep five standard MoE rescue families---Switch load-balance~\citep{fedus2022switch}, ST-MoE z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, entropy regularization, ReMoE ReLU routing~\citep{zhang2025remoe}, and expert-choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}---across eleven configurations on 6 datasets $\times$ 2 freeze levels $\times$ 5 seeds $= 720$ runs (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}, Appendix~\ref{app:rescue_details}). The best rescue (z-loss $c_z{=}0.01$) reduces MSE by only $10.9\%$, still $2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA. Excessive balancing ($\alpha{=}10.0$) is catastrophic ($+67.7\%$). This confirms Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii): when routing information is structurally absent from the hidden states, none of the standard rescue mechanisms we tested can compensate.
360:\textbf{The principle is architecture-agnostic.} RR-MoA is the minimal instantiation of a general principle: route on raw input. To confirm the bottleneck is in the routing \emph{input} rather than the router \emph{architecture}, we test two alternative instantiations. First, Self-Routed MoA (SR-MoA)~\citep{lv2025aoe,cheng2025ermoe,liu2026routingfree}: each expert contains its own sigmoid gate on raw input---no external router at all. SR-MoA \emph{outperforms} RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.464$; ETTm1: $0.388$; Weather: $0.222$; 252 runs total), generalizes across six backbones, and independently replicates the Frozen Paradox (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). That a different architecture exceeds RR-MoA while sharing only the raw-input principle confirms it is the \emph{principle}, not the specific router design, that drives the gains. The same SR-MoA architecture gating on hidden states degrades by $+87\%$ to $+768\%$ on \textbf{all 6 datasets} ($p{=}0.016$, Wilcoxon). \textbf{Normalization-specificity:} on Timer-XL (no RevIN), the same raw-vs-hidden comparison yields only $+4$--$9\%$---$15$--$100{\times}$ smaller than on MOMENT---confirming the degradation is normalization-induced. Second, replacing AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input router recovers entropy to $1.41$--$1.57$ and MSE by $41$--$88\%$ on all 12 cells (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}). All three instantiations (RR-MoA, SR-MoA, AdaMix-Raw) confirm the same diagnosis: the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Table~\ref{tab:causal_controls} summarizes all eight converging controls.
376:C6 & SR-MoA raw vs hidden & Generalizes beyond RR-MoA? & Hidden: $+87$--$768\%$ worse (Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}) \\
403:\textbf{RR-MoA (Top-2, frozen)} & $\mathbf{0.680 \pm 0.027}$ & $\mathbf{0.564 \pm 0.059}$ & $\mathbf{0.276 \pm 0.017}$ & --- \\
413:RR-MoA outperforms every baseline ($p{<}0.001$). The independent ensemble (same experts, no router) is $36$--$46\%$ worse, confirming learned routing adds value beyond diversity.
530:\legend{Full FT (unfrozen), Frozen RR-MoA}
566:\caption{\textbf{Left: Frozen Paradox}---frozen RR-MoA beats full FT by $12$--$79\%$. \textbf{Right: Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} validated} ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$). Traffic and Solar are boundary cases.}
572:{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Cross-backbone generalization.}\label{sec:cross_backbone} RR-MoA is not specific to MOMENT. On MOMENT-small and MOMENT-large (both using RevIN), it wins \textbf{all 21} configurations by $27$--$81\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:cross_backbone}). On Moirai (LayerNorm only, no RevIN), it wins \textbf{18/18} by $3$--$31\%$---demonstrating that raw-signal routing provides value \emph{beyond} the RevIN diagnosis: even when hidden states retain enough information to avoid collapse (Moirai entropy: $1.48$--$1.60$), the raw input carries richer per-window statistics that improve routing quality. On Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe}, which already contains sparse internal experts, RR-MoA still improves \textbf{all 6 datasets} by $37$--$90\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}), showing that adapter-level and backbone-internal routing operate on complementary axes. Two \textbf{negative controls} validate the diagnosis: Chronos and Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, which lack instance normalization, show no routing collapse (entropy $1.48$--$1.61$) and RR-MoA provides no advantage (\textbf{4/18} wins, within chance)---exactly as Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Appendix~\ref{app:cross_backbone}).}
575:Top-2 sparse routing adds $4.3$\,ms ($+10\%$) while retaining $63\%$ of the dense gain; scaling $K{=}3{\to}20$ changes MSE by ${<}5\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:topk}). RR-MoA generalizes to imputation ($7/8$ datasets; Appendix~\ref{app:imputation}).}
577:{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Multi-horizon generalization.} RR-MoA wins \textbf{24/24} configurations across $H{\in}\{96, 192, 336, 720\}$ on ETTh1, ETTm1, and Weather (5 seeds each; Table~\ref{tab:horizon}), with improvements of $27$--$49\%$ over the best fixed adapter at every horizon. The advantage is stable across horizon length: at $H{=}720$, RR-MoA still improves by $27$--$41\%$. A dual-stream extension (Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}, Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}) further extends this to all 6 datasets across 5 backbones and 4 horizons (Table~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb}).}
583:We identified \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse} as the root cause of MoE adapter failure on time series foundation models. Eight causal controls---including opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast})---isolate the mechanism, and a mutual-information decomposition predicts where it applies ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix principle is clear: \textbf{RR-MoA} routes on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} and a Frozen Paradox where frozen adapters outperform full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$. The diagnosis is further validated by its actionability: restoring raw-signal access to experts matches or beats DLinear on $107/123$ cells across six backbones.
932:\caption{\textbf{Multi-horizon RR-MoA vs.\ DLinear} (MOMENT-small, strictly frozen, Top-2, 5 seeds, test MSE mean$\pm$std). RR-MoA wins all 24 configurations vs.\ best fixed baseline across horizons $96$--$720$. DLinear column provides supervised calibration: the gap narrows from $+63\%$ to $+48\%$ on ETTh1 and from $+33\%$ to $+15\%$ on Weather as $H$ grows, consistent with the frozen backbone's horizon-invariant representation becoming relatively more informative at longer horizons.}
```

```
1280:\textbf{Instance-adaptive gating (IA-Gating).} In the dual-stream variant (Appendix~\ref{app:gap_closing}), we replace the static per-expert blending scalar $\alpha$ with a per-window gate $\gamma(X_\text{raw}) = \sigma(W_g \cdot z)$ where $z$ is the router's latent representation. Across 6 datasets (frozen, 3 seeds), IA-Gating wins on 4/6 (ETTh2 $-8.0\%$, ETTm2 $-6.4\%$, ETTm1 $-1.9\%$, Electricity $-0.4\%$) and loses on 2/6 (Weather $+6.1\%$, ETTh1 $+0.3\%$). The learned gates cluster tightly around $\gamma \approx 0.48$ across all datasets and windows, indicating the backbone's contribution is roughly constant per-window---which explains why the simpler static $\alpha$ performs comparably overall.
1945:\textbf{Why this matters for the diagnosis.} The fact that the gap closes precisely when experts recover the information our diagnosis identified as destroyed---and remains open when they cannot (FiLM re-injects only $\mu,\sigma$, yielding $+48\%$ on ETTh1 vs.\ $+9\%$ for dual-stream)---is direct evidence that the diagnosis is both \emph{correct} and \emph{actionable}. The normalization--encoding bottleneck is not merely an observation; it is the causal mechanism whose resolution closes the gap. Importantly, the frozen backbone and raw-routed paradigm remain unchanged---these variants extend the \emph{expert architecture}, not the routing mechanism, confirming that the routing diagnosis (the core contribution of this paper) is orthogonal to expert design.
1949:\textbf{Training-length ablation.} We additionally ran dual-stream at 50 epochs (vs.\ 15 in Table~\ref{tab:gap_closing}). Extended training \emph{overfits} on 5/6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.453{\to}0.556$; Weather: $0.198{\to}0.237$), confirming that dual-stream converges by 15 epochs and that the original training schedule is already near-optimal; additional adapter-only optimization past convergence degrades generalization due to the small effective parameter count ($\sim$718K trainable, frozen backbone).
1951:\subsection{Residual-IA: Diagnosing and Fixing a Second Pathology}
2083:\caption{\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} architecture (dual-stream extension).} \textit{Stream 1} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf{H}$, fed into each expert's Adapter head. \textit{Stream 2} (green): a shared NLinear branch reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ directly, producing $\mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw}$ — DLinear-equivalent and shared across all $K$ experts. Each expert combines them as $\mathbf{y}_k = \mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw} + \sigma(\mathrm{blend}_k(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw})) \cdot \mathrm{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$, with the blend gate initialized at $b{=}{-}2$ so the model starts as effectively-DLinear and learns to add backbone signal where useful. Self-routing $\sigma$ gates (orange) on $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ select which experts contribute. Result: \textbf{6/6 vs DLinear at $H{=}96$} on MOMENT-small; \textbf{107/123 cells} ($88\%$) match-or-beat across 6 backbones $\times$ 6 datasets $\times$ 4 horizons (Tables~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus}, \ref{tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb}).}

2231:\textbf{Implication.} Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} achieves \textbf{$107/123$ match-or-beat} ($88\%$) across six backbones, six datasets, and four horizons ($20/24$ MOMENT-small, $87/99$ cross-backbone; Table~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb}), with $65$ significant wins vs $11$ losses ($5.9{:}1$ ratio) and \textbf{6/6 at H${=}192$}. MOMENT-large reaches $23/24$ ($96\%$); Moirai-MoE achieves $15/15$ with $-9.4\%$ mean gap, confirming adapter-level routing stacks with backbone-internal MoE. Practitioners requiring a shared-TSFM deployment topology (Appendix~\ref{app:deployment}) now have an adapter that matches or beats per-tenant DLinear on $100\%$ of benchmarks at H${=}192$.
2235:The Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} result above is computed at H${=}96$. We extend to the full set of standard LTSF horizons to verify the result is not horizon-specific. A striking pattern emerges: the NLinear raw branch's advantage \emph{grows} with horizon length, precisely because non-stationarity (per-window level drift) compounds with the horizon. At H${=}720$ Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} wins ETTh2 by $-31.2\%$ (from $0.849$ to $0.584$, $p{=}0.023$).
2260:\subsubsection*{Cross-backbone generalization: does Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} depend on RevIN?}
2262:Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} was developed on MOMENT-small, which uses RevIN instance normalization. To test whether the recipe is RevIN-specific or transfers across normalization regimes, we re-run the full Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} config on four other backbones: Moirai (LayerNorm-only, no instance norm), Chronos (T5 encoder-decoder, no instance norm), MOMENT-large (RevIN, $24$ layers vs $8$), and Timer-XL (decoder-only, LayerNorm only).
```
