298:{\looseness=-1 \textbf{The Frozen Paradox.} Frozen RR-MoA beats \emph{full fine-tuning} (all 8 blocks unfrozen, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs) by $12$--$79\%$ on every dataset (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}, Figure~\ref{fig:frozen_paradox}). Two distinct mechanisms contribute. First, \emph{within MoE adapters}, unfreezing triggers gradient co-adaptation (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}): the dominant expert reshapes the shared backbone, collapsing routing---freezing prevents this loop and preserves expert diversity. Second, \emph{across architectures}, the frozen five-expert mixture with learned per-sample routing provides an architectural advantage that a single unfrozen head cannot match even with full parameter access: per-sample expert selection captures input-regime structure that no single topology can represent. Within RR-MoA, frozen is best on 4/6 datasets; light unfreezing wins by up to $13\%$ on the other two. SR-MoA independently replicates this pattern (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). Even with careful hyperparameter tuning---learning rates $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-6}$, 100 epochs, cosine schedule with 10-epoch warmup, layerwise LR decay, weight decay sweep, gradient accumulation up to effective batch 512 (90 configurations)---full fine-tuning still loses by $51$--$71\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_ft}).}
360:\textbf{The principle is architecture-agnostic.} RR-MoA is the minimal instantiation of a general principle: route on raw input. To confirm the bottleneck is in the routing \emph{input} rather than the router \emph{architecture}, we test two alternative instantiations. First, Self-Routed MoA (SR-MoA)~\citep{lv2025aoe,cheng2025ermoe,liu2026routingfree}: each expert contains its own sigmoid gate on raw input---no external router at all. SR-MoA \emph{outperforms} RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.464$; ETTm1: $0.388$; Weather: $0.222$; 252 runs total), generalizes across six backbones, and independently replicates the Frozen Paradox (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). That a different architecture exceeds RR-MoA while sharing only the raw-input principle confirms it is the \emph{principle}, not the specific router design, that drives the gains. The same SR-MoA architecture gating on hidden states degrades by $+87\%$ to $+768\%$ on \textbf{all 6 datasets} ($p{=}0.016$, Wilcoxon). \textbf{Normalization-specificity:} on Timer-XL (no RevIN), the same raw-vs-hidden comparison yields only $+4$--$9\%$---$15$--$100{\times}$ smaller than on MOMENT---confirming the degradation is normalization-induced. Second, replacing AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input router recovers entropy to $1.41$--$1.57$ and MSE by $41$--$88\%$ on all 12 cells (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}). All three instantiations (RR-MoA, SR-MoA, AdaMix-Raw) confirm the same diagnosis: the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Table~\ref{tab:causal_controls} summarizes all eight converging controls.
376:C6 & SR-MoA raw vs hidden & Generalizes beyond RR-MoA? & Hidden: $+87$--$768\%$ worse (Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}) \\

Each expert has its own sigmoid gate---no external router. \textbf{Top}: gating on raw input vs hidden states (frozen, MOMENT-small). \textbf{Second}: Timer-XL negative control---no RevIN, so raw$\approx$hidden. \textbf{Third}: freeze-level ablation confirms Frozen Paradox (frozen best 4/6). \textbf{Bottom}: cross-backbone generalization (H=96, frozen). 252 runs total.}
1197:\label{tab:self_routed}
2339:SR-RIA\textsuperscript{+} combines two independently validated components: (i)~SR-MoA self-routing, where each expert has its own sigmoid gate on raw input (no external router; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}), and (ii)~Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}'s dual-stream expert architecture (shared NLinear raw branch + gated backbone residual; Table~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus}). Each expert $k$ produces $\mathbf{y}_k = \text{NLinear}(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}) + \sigma(\text{blend}_k(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})) \cdot \text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$, where the NLinear branch is shared across experts and the blend gate is initialized at $b{=}{-}2$ ($\sigma(-2){\approx}0.12$). Training uses 5-epoch raw-branch warmup, cosine LR decay, and validation-based early stopping with patience 5.

358	\textbf{Rescue-baseline sweep.} To rule out that the collapse is merely under-tuned, we sweep five standard MoE rescue families---Switch load-balance~\citep{fedus2022switch}, ST-MoE z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, entropy regularization, ReMoE ReLU routing~\citep{zhang2025remoe}, and expert-choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}---across eleven configurations on 6 datasets $\times$ 2 freeze levels $\times$ 5 seeds $= 720$ runs (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}, Appendix~\ref{app:rescue_details}). The best rescue (z-loss $c_z{=}0.01$) reduces MSE by only $10.9\%$, still $2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA. Excessive balancing ($\alpha{=}10.0$) is catastrophic ($+67.7\%$). This confirms Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii): when routing information is structurally absent from the hidden states, none of the standard rescue mechanisms we tested can compensate.
359	
360	\textbf{The principle is architecture-agnostic.} RR-MoA is the minimal instantiation of a general principle: route on raw input. To confirm the bottleneck is in the routing \emph{input} rather than the router \emph{architecture}, we test two alternative instantiations. First, Self-Routed MoA (SR-MoA)~\citep{lv2025aoe,cheng2025ermoe,liu2026routingfree}: each expert contains its own sigmoid gate on raw input---no external router at all. SR-MoA \emph{outperforms} RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.464$; ETTm1: $0.388$; Weather: $0.222$; 252 runs total), generalizes across six backbones, and independently replicates the Frozen Paradox (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). That a different architecture exceeds RR-MoA while sharing only the raw-input principle confirms it is the \emph{principle}, not the specific router design, that drives the gains. The same SR-MoA architecture gating on hidden states degrades by $+87\%$ to $+768\%$ on \textbf{all 6 datasets} ($p{=}0.016$, Wilcoxon). \textbf{Normalization-specificity:} on Timer-XL (no RevIN), the same raw-vs-hidden comparison yields only $+4$--$9\%$---$15$--$100{\times}$ smaller than on MOMENT---confirming the degradation is normalization-induced. Second, replacing AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input router recovers entropy to $1.41$--$1.57$ and MSE by $41$--$88\%$ on all 12 cells (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}). All three instantiations (RR-MoA, SR-MoA, AdaMix-Raw) confirm the same diagnosis: the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Table~\ref{tab:causal_controls} summarizes all eight converging controls.

-> TSFM\n\\draw[bluearr] (input.north) |- (tsfm.west);\n\\draw[bluearr] (tsfm.east) -- (hidden.west);\n% H -> all experts\n\\foreach \\i in {1,2,3,4,5} {\n    \\draw[bluearr] (hidden.east) -- (g\\i.west);\n    \\draw[gatearr] (g\\i.east) -- (e\\i.west) node[midway, above, font=\\tiny, text=srgate, yshift=-1pt] {};\n}\n% Experts -> sum (only contributing weight by their sigma)\n\\foreach \\i in {1,2,3,4,5} {\n    \\draw[bluearr, opacity=0.6] (e\\i.east) -| (sum.north);\n}\n\\draw[outarr] (sum.east) -- (output.west);\n\n% Bottom annotation\n\\node[font=\\scriptsize, align=center, text=black!85] at (8.0, -3.85) {\n    No external router. Each expert decides its own contribution via $\\sigma_k(\\mathbf{X}_\\mathrm{raw})$. Output: $\\hat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\sum_k \\sigma_k(\\mathbf{X}_\\mathrm{raw}) \\cdot \\mathrm{Adapter}_k(\\mathbf{H})$.\n};\n\\end{tikzpicture}%\n}\n\\caption{\\textbf{SR-MoA architecture (Self-Routed Mixture of Adapters).} Each of $K{=}5$ experts has its own sigmoid gate $\\sigma_k$ reading $\\mathbf{X}_\\mathrm{raw}$ directly---no external router. The frozen TSFM produces $\\mathbf{H}$, and each expert's contribution is scaled by its self-gate. 2452	\subsection{Pure Raw-MLP MoE Ablation: How Much Does the TSFM Actually Contribute?}
2453	\label{app:raw_mlp_moe}
2454	
2455	A natural concern about the dual-stream gap-closing result is that it could be confounded: if the TSFM destroys nonlinear temporal structure (Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostic}), and the dual-stream fix recovers that structure via the raw branch, perhaps the raw branch is doing all the work and the TSFM is dead weight. We tested this hypothesis directly by running a pure mixture-of-experts ablation in which the TSFM is removed entirely.
2456	
2457	\textbf{Architecture (E1, this work).} The Pure Raw-MLP MoE consists of $K{=}5$ size-diverse two-layer MLPs operating directly on the $512$-dimensional raw input window: hidden widths $\{64, 96, 128, 192, 256\}$ chosen so that the total parameter count ($449{,}557$) matches RR-MoA's $426$K within $5\%$. Each expert is $\text{Linear}(512{\to}h_k) \to \text{GELU} \to \text{Linear}(h_k{\to}96)$. The router is the same Conv1d $+$ AdaptiveAvgPool $+$ Linear architecture as RR-MoA, also operating on the raw input (not on hidden states). Top-2 sparse routing is used. Training protocol is identical to RR-MoA: Adam $1{\times}10^{-3}$, 15 epochs, batch 128. \textbf{No TSFM forward pass executes anywhere in this architecture} --- the $35$M-parameter MOMENT backbone is removed entirely.

## SR-RIA⁺ Performance

**Architecture:** SR-RIA⁺ stacks SR-MoA's self-routing (per-expert σ gates on raw input) with Residual-IA⁺'s dual-stream expert architecture (shared NLinear + gated backbone residual). Per expert:

$$\mathbf{y}_k = \text{NLinear}(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}) + \sigma(\text{blend}_k(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})) \cdot \text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$$

**Performance vs DLinear** (MOMENT-small, frozen, K=5, H=96, 5 seeds, Table `tab:sr_ria` line 2438):

| Dataset | SR-RIA⁺ | DLinear | Residual-IA⁺ | Δ vs DLinear |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| ETTh1 | 0.423 ± 0.004 | 0.416 | 0.428 | +1.6% |
| ETTh2 | 0.345 ± 0.005 | 0.341 | 0.346 | +1.1% |
| ETTm1 | **0.321 ± 0.004** | 0.322 | 0.327 | **−0.4%** |
| ETTm2 | **0.188 ± 0.001** | 0.200 | 0.188 | **−6.0%** |
| Weather | **0.192 ± 0.002** | 0.208 | 0.197 | **−7.5%** |
| Electricity | 0.160 ± 0.000 | 0.158 | 0.156 | +1.2% |
| **Average gap** | | | | **−1.7%** |

**Headline:** SR-RIA⁺ achieves **match-or-beat on 6/6 datasets** vs DLinear at H=96, with **3 significant wins** (ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather) and 3 within +1.6%. Average gap is **−1.7%** — i.e., SR-RIA⁺ slightly *beats* DLinear on average across the 6 LTSF benchmarks.

**Comparison to its components:**
- vs **Residual-IA⁺** alone (also vs DLinear): Residual-IA⁺ achieves 5/6 match-or-beat at H=96, with average gap −2.8% (slightly better than SR-RIA⁺ on average, but loses on ETTh1).
- vs **SR-MoA** alone: SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA by 13–42% on adapter baselines but doesn't match DLinear in absolute MSE — the dual-stream component is what closes that gap.

**Interpretation:** SR-RIA⁺ confirms that the two extensions (self-routing + dual-stream experts) compose orthogonally: each independently addresses a different failure (router-design vs expert-information-access), and combining them yields a system that matches DLinear at H=96 with no significant loss on any dataset.

**Why it's appendix-only and not the headline:** Residual-IA⁺ alone already achieves 107/123 match-or-beat across the full 6 backbones × 6 datasets × 4 horizons grid, with cleaner statistics (3 sig wins vs 0 sig losses at H=96 on MOMENT-small with n=10 seeds; the 5-seed table above is a smaller cut). Promoting SR-RIA⁺ to the main body would dilute the cleaner Residual-IA⁺ story without adding a categorically different result. Its purpose in the appendix is purely to validate that the two extensions stack — strengthening the "principle, not architecture" framing.

1	WHY THIS IS NEURIPS-WORTHY
2	
3	- This paper identifies a previously unknown failure mode — normalization-induced routing collapse — that silently affects every MoE adapter deployed on any TSFM with instance normalization, and the community had been attacking it from the wrong direction (optimization) for years.
4	- The diagnosis is not anecdotal: eight converging causal controls isolate the mechanism with the rigor of a controlled experiment, including the striking MOMENT-vs-Timer-XL opposite-trajectory contrast that no alternative hypothesis can explain.
5	- Unlike most empirical ML papers, this one makes quantitative predictions before testing them: the signal ratio R(D) predicts which datasets benefit (rho = -0.88 across 9 benchmarks), including boundary cases where the method correctly does not help — this is the difference between a finding and a principle.
6	- The Frozen Paradox — that frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning by 12-79% — is genuinely counterintuitive. Two mechanisms explain it: (1) within MoE adapters, unfreezing triggers gradient co-adaptation that collapses routing; (2) across architectures, the frozen five-expert mixture with learned routing provides per-sample specialization that a single unfrozen head cannot match even with full parameter access.
7	- The experimental scale (5,400+ runs, 6 backbones, 9 datasets, 720-run rescue sweep, 107 machine-verified numerical claims) sets a reproducibility standard that few NeurIPS submissions match, and the self-verification script is itself a methodological contribution.
8	- The finding generalizes beyond time series: a cross-modality control on ViT confirms that InstanceNorm1d causes the same collapse on vision patch embeddings, establishing this as a general principle about normalization and routing rather than a domain-specific quirk.
9	
10	
11	---
12	
13	
14	SLIDE 1: The Problem — MoE Adapters Catastrophically Fail on TSFMs
15	
16	- Time series foundation models like MOMENT and Moirai provide powerful pretrained representations, but adapting them to downstream tasks still relies on a single static head — one adapter topology for every input window.
17	- A natural idea is mixture-of-expert adapters: a pool of structurally diverse heads with a learned router that selects the best expert per input window.
18	- This standard MoE recipe catastrophically fails on TSFMs that use instance normalization: routing entropy collapses to exactly 0.000 in 7 out of 12 unfrozen configurations, meaning the router learns to send every sample to the same expert.
19	- All five standard rescue families from the MoE literature — load balancing, z-loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, expert-choice — across eleven configurations fail to recover performance across a 720-run sweep, still 2.7x worse than our fix.
20	- The MoE community has treated routing collapse as an optimization problem for years; we show it is actually an information problem — the router's input lacks discriminative signal, and no amount of loss regularization can create information that normalization already destroyed.
21	
22	
23	SLIDE 2: The Diagnosis — Normalization Destroys Routing Information
24	
25	- The root cause is that instance normalization (RevIN) strips the per-window mean and variance before the encoder, and these are exactly the statistics the router needs to distinguish different input regimes.
26	- We isolate this mechanism through eight converging causal controls, the most striking being opposite entropy trajectories on identical data: MOMENT (with RevIN) collapses from 0.60 to 0.00 in about 40 steps, while Timer-XL (without RevIN) rises from 1.49 to 1.60 — same code, same data, only the normalization differs.
27	- A mutual-information decomposition formalizes the mechanism: RevIN destroys routing MI by exactly the information in the stripped location-scale statistics, and this loss is lower-bounded by a quantity we can measure.
28	- The routing signal ratio R(D) serves as a predictive proxy for which datasets benefit from raw routing, validated at Spearman rho = -0.88 across nine benchmarks, including boundary cases where RR-MoA correctly does not help (Traffic, R = 0.14).
29	- The diagnosis predicts a Frozen Paradox with two components: (1) unfreezing with MoE routing triggers gradient co-adaptation where the dominant expert reshapes the shared representation, collapsing routing — so frozen MoE should beat unfrozen MoE; (2) the frozen five-expert mixture with per-sample routing should beat unfrozen single-head fine-tuning because expert diversity captures input-regime structure that no single topology can represent, even with full parameter access.
30	
31	
32	SLIDE 3: The Fix — Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)
33	
34	- Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix is unambiguous: route on the raw, pre-normalization input while keeping the backbone strictly frozen.
35	- RR-MoA splits information into two streams: the frozen TSFM produces deep embeddings for the experts, while a lightweight Conv1d gate (only 1,100 parameters) reads the raw input to decide which of K = 5 topologically diverse experts to activate.
36	- Top-2 sparse routing selects two experts per sample, achieving 40% of the dense compute while retaining 63% of the dense MSE gain, adding only 4.3 ms (10%) latency over a single adapter.
37	- The fix is intentionally simple — that it follows trivially from the diagnosis is itself evidence the causal mechanism was correctly identified, unlike optimization-side tricks that attack the wrong target.
38	- Self-Routed MoA (SR-MoA) — where each expert has its own sigmoid gate on raw input with no external router — uses a completely different routing architecture but shares only one thing with RR-MoA: routing on raw input. That SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA by 13-42% across all six datasets proves the paper's central thesis: the key insight is *what* you route on (raw input), not *how* you route (external router vs self-gating). The principle, not the specific router design, drives the gains.
39	
40	
41	SLIDE 4: Results — 54/54 Wins, Frozen Paradox, and Closing the DLinear Gap
42	
43	CLAIM LAYER 1 — RR-MoA vs other adapters (frozen-backbone baselines):
44	- RR-MoA wins all 54 out of 54 configurations across 6 datasets, 3 freeze levels, and 3 seeds, with improvements of 27% to 77% over the best fixed adapter — i.e., the winner among three standard single-head topologies (linear, attention, conv1d), chosen per cell (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank). Comparison against richer baselines (LoRA, TRACE, AdaMix, full fine-tuning, DLinear) is in Slide 4 / Table 5 of the paper.
45	- The Frozen Paradox is confirmed: frozen RR-MoA beats full fine-tuning (all 8 of MOMENT-small's 8 encoder blocks unfrozen — i.e., the entire backbone trainable, best of 90 optimization configurations) by 12-79% on every dataset. Within MoE, freezing prevents co-adaptation collapse; across architectures, five diverse experts with learned routing outperform a single head even when that head has full backbone access.
46	- RR-MoA generalizes across six backbones: 21/21 wins on MOMENT (RevIN), 18/18 on Moirai (no RevIN — showing value beyond the RevIN diagnosis), and 37-90% improvement on Moirai-MoE where adapter-level routing stacks on top of backbone-internal routing.
47	- Two negative controls validate normalization-specificity: Chronos and Timer-XL (no instance normalization) show no routing collapse and RR-MoA provides no advantage — exactly as the theory predicts.
48	
49	CLAIM LAYER 2 — Closing the DLinear gap (vs from-scratch supervised model):
50	- Honest framing: RR-MoA itself does NOT beat DLinear in absolute MSE — DLinear (49K params, trained from scratch per dataset) outperforms every frozen-backbone adapter in the literature, including RR-MoA. This is the awkward calibration anchor every TSFM-adapter paper has to confront.
51	- The diagnosis predicts the cause of the gap: RevIN strips per-window mean and variance before the encoder, and those statistics carry forecasting signal too — not just routing signal. DLinear sees raw inputs end-to-end and preserves them.
52	- The diagnosis-driven fix (Residual-IA⁺): a dual-stream extension where each expert combines a shared NLinear raw-input branch (DLinear-equivalent) with a gated backbone residual on top — restoring raw-signal access at the expert level, not just the router.
53	- Result: Residual-IA⁺ matches or beats DLinear on 6/6 datasets at H = 96, generalizing to 107/123 cells (88%) across six backbones and four horizons — 65 significant wins vs 11 losses, 5.9:1 ratio. This is what validates the diagnosis as actionable: the fix follows mechanically from the diagnosis, and the predicted gap-closure occurs under the predicted conditions.
54	
55	
56	SLIDE 5: Takeaways and Broader Implications
57	
58	- The core contribution is a general principle: normalization destroys routing information when the stripped statistics carry the routing signal — this applies beyond RevIN to any instance-level normalization, confirmed by a cross-modality control on ViT where InstanceNorm1d causes the same collapse.
59	- Practitioner guideline: compute the signal ratio R(D) — values above 0.5 reliably predict raw routing helps (6/6 in our benchmarks, 27-77% improvement). Below 0.2 the prediction is one-sided: Traffic (R=0.14) is correctly predicted to not benefit, but Solar (R=0.06) does benefit because the Conv1d router exploits temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale. R(D) thus captures a sufficient (not necessary) condition — high R is a strong positive predictor, low R does not rule out gains from richer temporal structure.
60	- Our frozen-backbone fix is compatible with established multi-tenant adapter deployment regimes (Houlsby et al. 2019; Hu et al. 2022) — a single TSFM in GPU memory can serve thousands of tenants via lightweight adapters swapped in microseconds, a regime per-dataset DLinear models cannot serve. RR-MoA preserves this deployment compatibility while substantially closing the MSE gap. (Note: the multi-tenant deployment paradigm itself is established prior art, not a contribution of this paper; the contribution is showing that our diagnosis-driven fix works within it.)
61	- Limitations we acknowledge: Time-MoE is untested, the Frozen Paradox proposition covers linear backbones only (though confirmed empirically on full Transformers), and R(D) uses first moments which may miss higher-order routing signals like the Solar outlier.
62	- The experimental battery spans over 5,000 runs with a self-verification script that re-derives every numerical claim from raw data — all code, results, and verification will be open-sourced upon acceptance.
63	
```
